Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette:
Mateo presents as a sharp, articulate 22-year-old, though his posture is rigid, his shoulders held tight against the back of the chair. He is six months removed from a traumatic event that occurred during a family visit to his parents' home country. He had been there for a wedding, a joyous occasion that was shattered in an instant. While walking through a bustling open-air market with his cousins, a car bomb detonated two stalls down from where they were haggling over textiles. Mateo remembers the sound being swallowed by a sudden, violent pressure change, a force that threw him off his feet. What haunts him most, he explains, is not the explosion itself but the chaotic, silent surge of movement that followed-the blur of bodies running, falling, and the terrifying sensation of being trampled before he could scramble to his feet. He was physically unharmed, save for a few scrapes, but the world has not felt solid since.

Upon returning to his fast-paced job as a Product Manager in a tech company, Mateo tried to bury the experience. He was safe in his sleek, open-plan office, thousands of miles away. But safety felt like a concept, not a reality. His body remained on high alert, a tightly coiled spring of tension in his neck and back. He found himself unable to focus during team stand-ups, his attention constantly pulled from the project board to the movement in the periphery-a developer walking behind him, a designer gesturing emphatically. Each unexpected motion sent a jolt of adrenaline through him, a physical recoil so pronounced that he once knocked his laptop off its stand when a colleague approached his desk from behind. He was certain that any sudden movement signaled an imminent, catastrophic impact. This deep-seated fear has made his collaborative work environment feel like a minefield.

To manage the overwhelming waves of panic, Mateo developed a series of rituals. He constantly monitors his own body, checking his pulse under the desk during meetings, convinced that the frantic beating in his chest is a sign of a heart attack, not fear. He feels for tremors in his hands before a presentation, interpreting any slight shake as proof that he is physically breaking down. When the feeling becomes unbearable, usually after a startling encounter at work, he retreats to the bathroom. There, he will dig his fingernails hard into the palm of his other hand, focusing on the sharp, localized pain until the roaring in his ears subsides. It's the only thing that seems to cut through the terror and make him feel real again. The relief is fleeting. He finds himself calling his older sister multiple times a day, his voice low and urgent. "I just felt weird, do I sound okay?" he'll ask, needing her to confirm his sanity, to reassure him that he is not, in fact, dying or losing his mind.

The constant vigilance is exhausting. He has started taking longer routes through the office to avoid crowded areas and often positions his chair so his back is firmly against a solid wall, limiting the possibility of being surprised. His manager has commented on his recent "jumpiness" and a noticeable dip in his engagement with the team. It was after his sister, her voice strained with worry, finally told him, "Mateo, I can't be your doctor. I love you, but you need to talk to someone who can actually help," that he made the call. He has come to therapy because he is terrified of losing the career he has worked so hard to build. More than that, he is desperate to inhabit his own body without feeling like it is a constant, screaming alarm.
